🤖 THREEHALVES — THE CENTAUR ROBOT Threehalves is a 7-foot-tall teleoperated robot developed by Satyress. Its design combines a human-like torso and arms with a powerful four-legged chassis, creating a mechanical centaur built for environments that are too dangerous for humans. The idea behind Threehalves is simple: instead of sending a person into extreme heat, unstable terrain, darkness, hazardous industrial environments or disaster zones, a skilled operator can control the robot remotely and perform the work from a safer location. Unlike many humanoid robots, Threehalves is designed around tools and equipment that humans already use. Its modular limbs and quick-connect system allow it to be adapted for different tasks, while its four-legged platform provides stability on difficult terrain. The most unsettling part is probably its appearance. With its enormous size, humanoid body, four mechanical legs and distinctive horned head, Threehalves looks less like a traditional industrial machine and more like something from a science-fiction horror movie. But behind the terrifying design is a serious engineering concept: putting the machine in danger instead of the human. Threehalves is still a developing robotics project, but it represents a strange glimpse into a future where dangerous jobs could be performed remotely — with a human controlling the machine from a distance. And honestly… it might be one of the creepiest robots ever built. 👁️ #threehalves #robot #baal #satyress #horrortok

Chinese humanoid robots broke records set by humans, including Usain Bolt's 100m sprint world record, on the opening day of the Olympics-like World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing on Saturday. More than 2,000 humanoid robots were participating in the event, organisers said. In a 100-metre sprint, a humanoid robot achieved a result of 9.39 seconds, beating the human record of 9.58 seconds set by Jamaican athlete Bolt in 2009. In a standing high jump, a humanoid robot was able to reach 2.88m, well above the 0.95m best result by a humanoid in last year’s first edition of the games. It surpassed the human high jump record of 2.45m set by Cuba’s Javier Sotomayor in 1993. The five-day games, now in their second year, are a spectacle demonstrating China’s rapid progress in advanced robotics as the technology race with the US heats up. There are 51 events and more than 1,000 competitions taking place, including running, table tennis and football. For more news, visit @sbsnews_au (link in bio).

This is an art exhibit called “Can’t Help Myself.”
 It’s programmed to try to contain the hydraulic fluid that’s constantly leaking out and required to
 keep itself running - If too much escapes, it will die.
 The saddest part is that the creators gave the robot the ability to do ‘happy dances’ for
 spectators while the spill was contained.
 When the project was first launched in 2016 it danced around spending most of its time
 interacting with the crowd since it could quickly pull back the small spillage.
 Over time, the leak was designed to get worse.
 By the time this video was taken, the leaking fluid had become unmanageable.
 The robot no longer has any time to dance as it struggles desperately to keep itself alive, living its
 last days in a never-ending cycle between sustaining life and bleeding out.
 I think the reason this demonstration hits so hard is because it’s a feeling we can all relate to.
 Earlier in life, we had the time and the energy to be creative and spend time with our loved ones.
 Now, as time goes on, not only do we need to work harder to support ourselves… But thanks to
 economic changes, it’s getting more and more difficult, and for many people the situation is
 becoming desperate.
 But - people aren’t robots.
 We have the ability to recognize our situation and change our programming.

XPENG’s humanoid robot, known as IRON, represents the company’s expansion beyond electric vehicles into robotics and embodied AI. XPENG, a Chinese EV manufacturer founded in 2014, has leveraged its expertise in electric drivetrains, AI software, and autonomous systems to develop robotic platforms capable of dynamic movement and real-time environmental interaction. Humanoid robots like IRON rely on advanced motion planning algorithms, electric actuators, and sensor fusion systems - typically combining cameras, LiDAR, inertial measurement units (IMUs), and force sensors. These systems allow the robot to maintain balance, adjust posture, and perform coordinated movements that appear fluid and human-like. Modern humanoid locomotion depends heavily on real-time feedback control. Small positional corrections are made hundreds of times per second to stabilize joints and prevent falls. This is similar to the control architecture used in self-balancing robots and autonomous vehicles. XPENG’s broader robotics initiative aligns with a global push toward general-purpose humanoid platforms - machines designed to operate in human environments rather than factory-only settings. While still in early development stages, such robots are being researched for applications ranging from logistics and manufacturing to service roles and human-robot interaction studies. I spent days teaching a 3D-printed robot duck to walk. Most of that time, it was falling over. It’s my own build of the Open Duck Mini. The open-source, BDX-inspired biped created by Antoine Pirrone. The whole thing is 3D-printed and runs on hobby-grade servos instead of industrial actuators, which is what makes it buildable on a normal budget and also what makes it so hard to get walking. The hard part wasn’t the printing or the assembly. It was the sim-to-real gap. A gait that walks perfectly in MuJoCo hits real-world joint slop, servo lag, and a center of mass that won’t sit still, and just before you know it, the duck face plants into the floor. It took me 40+ calibration passes before it could take three steps without tipping! What the build came down to: • 3D-printed chassis • Per-joint offset calibration (where most of the pain lived) • Policy training in simulation (MuJoCo / Isaac Lab) • Build guide + docs via Tnkr • A lot of failed walks Real hardware. Real failures. Real progress.

You can now buy a humanoid robot for $4K Humanoid robots just got insanely cheap, and this might change everything. In this video, we break down how Unitree Robotics just launched a $4,000 humanoid robot on AliExpress, a price point that was unthinkable just a few years ago. The R1 robot stands 123cm tall and can perform advanced movements like cartwheels, running downhill, and getting back up on its own. What’s wild? Robots with similar capabilities used to cost anywhere from $50,000 to $150,000, meaning prices have dropped by over 90%. Even more surprising, China is already dominating the humanoid robotics race. While companies like Tesla, Figure AI, and Agility Robotics have only shipped around 150 units each, Unitree has already shipped over 5,500 robots. What used to live in research labs and sci-fi movies is now available to anyone with a credit card, on the same platform you would use to buy everyday gadgets. So the real question is what happens when humanoid robots become this affordable? Drop your thoughts in the comments and subscribe for more content on the future of tech, AI, and innovation.

A lot of attention is going to general-purpose humanoid robots like Figure 3 and Tesla Optimus. These are the do-it-all machines, similar to how SUVs became the dominant car type because they can handle many different needs. But that will likely be only one part of the market.  As the industry grows, different kinds of robots could fill different roles. Industrial robots like Boston Dynamics Atlas could become the workhorses built for hard labor and demanding jobs. Softer, friendlier designs from companies like Fauna Robotics and Sunday Robotics could represent a more family-friendly category made to feel safer and less intimidating around people and kids.  There may also be a market for robots built more for fun, status, or entertainment than pure usefulness, like the sports cars of robotics. And if robots really become common, the industry will need much more than just the machines themselves. It will need repair services, upgrades, customization, and resale markets too, just like cars do.  If robotics is going to become a real part of everyday life, it will likely need multiple segments and a full support system around it.#robotics #ainews #Techtok #futuretech #autonomous

Microduck is one of the most accessible open-source biped robots launched in 2026. Built by Pollen Robotics, the robotics team at Hugging Face, Microduck is a 25 cm open-source biped robot priced at $399, designed for robotics research, embodied AI, robot learning and locomotion experiments. The small robot weighs under 800 g and uses 15 motors, a camera, depth sensing, dual IMUs and an articulated beak. In the launch demo, Microduck walks, squats, picks objects from the floor, recovers after losing balance and stands back up after different types of falls. Its low price makes it especially interesting for developers, robotics students and AI researchers who want to experiment with biped locomotion, balance control, manipulation, reinforcement learning, embodied intelligence and physical AI without buying a full-size humanoid robot. Microduck also supports wheels attached to its feet, giving researchers another way to study mobile manipulation and hybrid robot locomotion. The gap between expensive humanoid robotics labs and affordable open-source robot platforms keeps getting smaller. WATCH: Figure Al Humanoid Robots Are Casually Walking Around Silicon Valley Figure Al humanoid robots have been spotted casually walking and standing outside the company's headquarters in San Jose, creating a scene that looks straight out of science fiction. The robots are part of Figure's growing Figure 03 fleet, powered by the company's Helix Al system for autonomous movement and real world tasks. Figure has been rapidly scaling production while deploying its humanoids into real environments including manufacturing facilities, where they are learning to perform physical work alongside humans. But seeing several humanoids simply hanging around a sunny Silicon Valley plaza feels different. The robot future is starting to look surprisingly normal. Credit: Figure Al

XPeng just built a factory where robots assemble other robots and this robot was the first one to walk out on its own legs Meet IRON a full-size humanoid robot built by XPeng It runs on three chips XPeng built itself so the AI runs on the robot instead of on a server somewhere or a person controlling it remotely And the factory building these robots is the real game changer Humanoid robots have mostly been built a few at a time with people putting them together by hand Usually engineers built robots in a lab Because of this each robot was a little different from the one before it XPengs main business is electric cars so they built the robot factory the same way they build vehicle lines Over eighty percent of the assembly line is automated because its built on the same standards they use for their vehicles And what XPeng did next shows where theyre taking this At the ceremony XPengs CEO clipped a staff badge onto the robot Not as a joke An actual employee badge on a machine But the craziest part Robots building robots can be efficient and precise But it also raises the question of whether theyll need us at all Hashtags: #XPeng #IRON #XPengFactory #IRONRobotsBuildRobots
